account: Superpower Glass, developed at Stanford University, runs a machine-learning facial-expression classifier on Google Glass. It shows a child which emotion a facing person is displaying. An at-home feasibility study took in children between July and October 2016. In it, 14 children with autism completed the protocol. The feasibility paper reports a 7.14-point reduction on the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2) in its abstract and from its published means. Its results prose gives 7.38 points. Twelve of 14 families reported more eye contact (npj Digital Medicine, 2018). A randomized trial enrolled 71 children aged 6 to 12 from 1 November 2016 to 11 April 2018. Those adding the device to applied behavioral analysis therapy gained 4.58 points more on the Vineland socialization subscale than controls (P = .005). Three other primary measures did not reach significance (JAMA Pediatrics, 2019). Results are cohort-level. Spectrum reported on 2 May 2019 that independent autism researchers judged the trial weak and that the Vineland gain had disappeared six weeks after treatment ended. Spectrum also reported that Cognoa held an exclusive license from Stanford and breakthrough status from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the therapy. A 2024 systematic review by University of Sydney researchers rated the trial at low risk of bias. The reviewers flagged potential funding bias and noted that children in the trial used the device about half as often as recommended. No source reports that Superpower Glass reached the market.

ai_role.statement: The emotion classifier, trained on public facial-expression databases and tuned for home conditions, generates the real-time cues the intervention relies on. The Guess the Emotion game within the package does not use the classifier. So part of the effect may come from structured family interaction rather than the AI.

fields.headline: Superpower Glass briefly raises social scores of children with autism
fields.title: Stanford's Superpower Glass gives children with autism emotion cues on Google Glass and raises a socialization score that fades after treatment

provenance.basis: SHA-256 of the public case, its assessments, and its displayed answers and notes, excluding its own identifier and the derived coverage summary.

value.role: SHA-256 of the complete public case and its assessments

fields.account: Superpower Glass, developed at Stanford University, runs a machine-learning facial-expression classifier on Google Glass. It shows a child which emotion a facing person is displaying. An at-home feasibility study took in children between July and October 2016. In it, 14 children with autism completed the protocol. The feasibility paper reports a 7.14-point reduction on the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2) in its abstract and from its published means. Its results prose gives 7.38 points. Twelve of 14 families reported more eye contact (npj Digital Medicine, 2018). A randomized trial enrolled 71 children aged 6 to 12 from 1 November 2016 to 11 April 2018. Those adding the device to applied behavioral analysis therapy gained 4.58 points more on the Vineland socialization subscale than controls (P = .005). Three other primary measures did not reach significance (JAMA Pediatrics, 2019). Results are cohort-level. Spectrum reported on 2 May 2019 that independent autism researchers judged the trial weak and that the Vineland gain had disappeared six weeks after treatment ended. Spectrum also reported that Cognoa held an exclusive license from Stanford and breakthrough status from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the therapy. A 2024 systematic review by University of Sydney researchers rated the trial at low risk of bias. The reviewers flagged potential funding bias and noted that children in the trial used the device about half as often as recommended. No source reports that Superpower Glass reached the market.

ratings.reason: Children in the trial's device group gained 4.58 points more on the parent-reported Vineland socialization subscale than controls, a measured improvement in a test score. Spectrum reported that the gain had disappeared six weeks after treatment ended, so no lasting change is documented.
The device was used only in research cohorts, and no source reports a change across a population.
